summary: This RFC reviews proposals for letting one Internet network number stand for a group of physical networks under common administration. This hides internal complexity from the rest of the Internet and describes another subnet addressing scheme.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 936 describes a way for one Internet network number to cover several internal physical networks. Local hosts use part of the host address to identify a subnet, while outside systems see one network.

questions: how can one network number cover several physical networks
subtitle: A subnet scheme that marks local subnets within the host part of an Internet address.

tldr.problem: Organizations need to divide a physical network into locally routed subnets without exposing every internal network to the wider Internet.
tldr.mechanism: For locally administered networks, the high-order bit of the host field distinguishes a subnet address from an address on the main network.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes the Berkeley scheme, in which internal subnet routes are visible locally but the collection appears as one network externally.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 936's status as Unknown. The RFC describes a Berkeley subnet scheme and compares it with other addressing proposals.

sections.title: Hiding Internal Network Complexity
sections.content:
Subnetting lets an organization treat several physical networks under common administration as one network from the rest of the Internet. Internal hosts and gateways can route among the subnets, while outside systems need only a common route to the organization.

This arrangement localizes configuration changes and avoids needing a new network number for every new cable. The RFC describes an alternative subnet scheme that had been used at the University of California, Berkeley since April 1984.
sections.plainLanguage: An organization can divide its network internally while presenting one network to the outside. Internal routing handles the extra structure.

sections.title: Finding a Subnet in the Host Address
sections.content:
For locally controlled networks, hosts inspect the host part of an Internet address. If its high-order bit is set, the rest of the high-order byte identifies the subnet; if the bit is clear, the address is interpreted normally as part of the main network.

The scheme uses an 8-bit subnet field for Class A and Class B networks. Class C networks are not included in the current scheme; the RFC discusses a possible 4-bit subnet field as an alternative for them.
sections.plainLanguage: On a local network, one bit tells a host whether the address identifies a subnet. Other bits then identify which subnet it means.

sections.title: Local Routes, Single External Network
sections.content:
The Berkeley implementation treats the subnet field as an extension of the network field for routing. Within the organization, subnets appear as separate networks with their own routing entries; outside it, they remain invisible and look like one network.

The RFC compares this design with other proposals and notes a trade-off: reserving half of the host addresses for subnet use leaves fewer addresses for the main network, while the fixed subnet-field width simplifies address interpretation.
sections.plainLanguage: Local routers can distinguish and route to separate subnets. Other networks do not need to know those internal details.
